Abstract
Interconnection networks are playing an increasingly crucial role
in achieving scalability and throughput for post-exascale and zettas-
cale computing systems. Resource consumption characteristics of
AI and HPC workloads are essential to designing effective network
infrastructure. The operation practice of production supercomput-
ing systems reveals that small and medium-sized jobs consume
most compute-core hours, generating traffic that mainly utilizes
a size-restricted portion of the network. Unfortunately, current
topologies lack sufficient support for flexible partitioning of dis-
tinct concurrent jobs. This study bridges this gap by exploring a
new tradeoff among scalability, throughput, and non-blocking re-
gions. We present Zettafly, a family of low-diameter topologies
with large-scale non-blocking sub-networks, allowing the majority
of jobs to be isolated within a single sub-network. Zettafly is a
two-layer structure, consisting of non-blocking groups and global
routers, such that each minimally routed packet between groups
traverses at most one global router. We also introduce simple and
efficient adaptive routing algorithms for Zettafly. We conduct exten-
sive simulations and analysis to evaluate the performance and cost
of Zettafly against state-of-the-art topologies. The results show that
Zettafly achieves great performance under typical HPC workloads,
offers cost-effectiveness under multi-task mixed traffic, supports
flexible configurations and incremental deployments, and is cost-
effective to deploy for post-exascale and zettascale systems.

Introduction
With the increasing demand for AI and HPC systems, the era of
large-scale interconnection systems is approaching. The large-scale
AI system Colossus [8], deployed by xAI with over 100,000 H100
GPUs under a 400 Gbps network bandwidth, has recently been put
into operation. Topology design is critical in constructing intercon-
nection systems, as it largely determines network performance and
cost [34]. Efficient topology design must consider key metrics such
as, low diameter, high bandwidth, scalability, and cost-effectiveness.
To achieve zettascale computing, a large-scale interconnection sys-
tem with 100,000 nodes may be required. However, existing topolo-
gies still have room for improvement in balancing the above metrics
when constructing such large systems.
Many topologies with solid theoretical foundations and cost-
effectiveness have been proposed. However, their implementation
in large-scale systems is constrained by limited scalability or com-
plex network structures. When using 64-port routers, networks
with a diameter of 2, such as Slim Fly [14], MLFM [1, 32], and Po-
larfly [35], can support only tens of thousands of nodes. Due to the
complexity of the network structures, some topologies with good
scalability, like Galaxyfly [38], Bundlefly [37], and Polarstar [36], are
challenging to deploy and maintain on a large scale. HammingMesh
[25] is designed for ring communication in deep learning, offering
excellent cost-effectiveness. Nonetheless, it has limitations in terms
of scalability and bisection bandwidth.
Some well-established classic topologies do not exhibit good
network performance or cost-effectiveness when deployed on a
large scale. High-dimensional torus or torus-like topologies [12]
are scalable and have been deployed [29]. However, these torus

However, their network performance is susceptible to global band-
width constraints and network noise. Production-level Dragonfly
systems typically distribute jobs larger than one group across the
network to mitigate global bandwidth constraints [13]. However,
combined with adaptive routing, this distribution can generate sig-
nificant network noise and potentially slow down the system by
up to twofold [19]. Moreover, designing precise adaptive routing in
Dragonfly is challenging, as discussed in Section 3.3, and is crucial
to network performance. Fat-tree is the predominant topology in
current AI and HPC systems. Constructing a maximum 3-level non-
blocking fat-tree network using the 64-port 400Gbps InfiniBand
switches would cost approximately hundreds of millions of dollars
and can accommodate only 65,536 nodes. To interconnect a system
with over 100,000 nodes, a 4-level fat-tree network may be neces-
sary, which would lead to prohibitively expensive network costs.
An oversubscribed fat-tree can effectively reduce costs. However,
it significantly impacts network performance and offers limited
improvements to scalability.
The goal of this paper is to design a topology that strikes a
good balance among low diameter, cost-effectiveness, scalability,
and high bandwidth, while also providing effective job isolation.
This involves the following main challenges: (1) ensuring good
scalability and reasonable network cost to support post-exascale
and zettascale computing; (2) providing a network structure that is
easy to package and deploy; and (3) constructing sufficiently large
non-blocking regions (NBRs) to isolate the majority of small- and
medium-scale jobs. A key constraint in deploying Dragonfly and
any other 𝑓𝑙𝑖𝑒𝑠in AI systems is that it only provides NBRs of limited
size and very few shortest paths connecting these NBRs. An NBR
refers to a region where sufficient network bandwidth is provided
so that nodes within the region can achieve saturated bandwidth
for any non-hotspot traffic pattern. Obviously, NBRs represent the
ideal network environment for any job. While a full-bisection fat-
tree provides NBR across its entire network, Dragonfly only offers
NBRs at the group level. For HyperX [12], NBRs are even smaller
and exist only at the router level. Whether in AI or HPC systems,
the majority of total GPU/CPU runtime is consumed by small to
medium-sized jobs, and the traffic generated by these jobs typically
utilizes only a limited portion of the network. Figure 1 illustrates
the distribution relationship between core hours and job size across
four systems in 2023 [6, 7]. Among these systems, Seren and Kalos
[27] are GPU data centers specifically designed for large language
model training, while Theta [11] and Polaris [9] are supercomputers
operated by Argonne National Laboratory. Notably, approximately
70% of the core hours are consumed by small to medium-sized jobs
that occupied less than 30% of the system’s nodes. This indicates
that providing expensive full-bisection bandwidth between any two
nodes in a fat-tree network is unnecessary. However, as shown in
Figure 2, other topologies provide at least two orders of magnitude
smaller NBRs than fat-tree.
To address the above challenges, by incorporating the character-
istics of the job size in real systems, we propose Zettafly, a two-layer
indirect topology composed of multiple large non-blocking sub-
networks (SNs). Each SN consists of multiple non-blocking groups,
where each group can adopt a fully connected network as in Drag-
onfly, or a two-level fat-tree structure as in Megafly. This design

Zettafly Topology
Zettafly, inspired by Dragonfly [34], Megafly [23, 42], and MLFM
[1, 32], is designed to be a generalized two-level indirect topology
comprising multiple low-diameter non-blocking local groups and
global routers, while ensuring that at least one global router exists
to directly connect any two groups. Although these local groups
can be arbitrary low-diameter non-blocking networks, our design
focuses on two group structures: a fully connected network and
a two-level fat-tree, as shown in Figure 3 (a) and (b). When fully
connected networks (or two-level fat-trees) are chosen as groups,
Zettafly guarantees a low diameter of 3 (or 4), simply denoted as
Zettafly-3 (or Zettafly-4, respectively). We further introduce the
non-blocking sub-networks in Zettafly. Zettafly comprises multiple
SNs, where each SN comprises multiple groups and is connected
through a uniform number of global routers, denoted as GR, shown
in Figure 3. Each global router bridges two SNs, and its ports are
equally divided between them. As shown in Figure 3 (b), one SN in
Zettafly-4 resembles a three-level fat-tree, where half of the ports on
its root switches are dangling. Global routers of Zettafly-4, bridging
two SNs, can be regarded as the shared root switches of two three-
layer fat-trees. Therefore, it is clear that each SN is non-blocking.
Next, we will present the mathematical definition of Zettafly and its
theoretical analysis. Table 1 presents the symbols used in this paper.

3) Bisection bandwidth: The bisection cut is defined as the
minimum number of connections that need to be cut to divide the
network into two equal parts, with each part containing the same
number of nodes. ZF is a symmetrical topology, with non-blocking
bandwidth within its SNs, but relatively fewer links between SNs.
Therefore, the minimum bisection cut for ZF divides the network
into two parts, each containing the same number of SNs. Figure 4
(c) shows the comparison of bisection bandwidth across different
topologies, which is calculated by dividing the number of severed
links by the number of network nodes. Zettafly, similar to DF, MF,
and HX-3, achieves a bisection bandwidth ratio of 0.25.
4) Topology resiliency: We simulate random link failures in the
network to analyze the resilience of ZF. Figures 4 (c) and (d) illus-
trate how the network diameter and average path length vary with
the link failure rate when the number of nodes (N) is approximately
1000. For indirect topologies, we only measure the distance between
routers connected to the nodes. Overall, ZF achieves resilience com-
parable to that of Dragonfly and Metafly, with disconnection rates
between 60% and 65%. However, due to the extremely scarce global
links between groups, the network diameter in DF and MF increases
more rapidly than in ZF at low link failure rates (e.g., 0.05). With
their abundant path diversity, FT-3 and HX-3 exhibit the best re-
silience, albeit at the cost of lower scalability.

3
Routing
We now discuss the minimal and non-minimal routing for ZF and
propose Valiant [44] routing and Sub-Network Adaptive Load Bal-
ancing (SNAL) routing, which are suitable for ZF. We demonstrate
how ZF ensures deadlock freedom. We also show the advantages
of SNAL in job isolation, congestion awareness, and resource con-
sumption. Due to its two-level fat-tree intra-group structure, the
routing algorithms on ZF-4 are simpler than that of ZF-3. We will
first introduce the routing on ZF-4, followed by ZF-3.
3.1
Routing for Zettafly-4
1) Minimal random routing: The yellow path in Figure 5 illus-
trates the minimal routing scheme. In this scheme, packets are
transmitted along the shortest paths from the source router to the
destination router. When both routers are located within the same
SN, the upward ports for the packet can be chosen randomly at
each step. However, if the source and destination routers belong
to different SNs, the packet can only select the unique port at the
𝐿1 router that leads to the destination SN. Minimal routing can be
described as moving either towards or away from the global router
or the 𝐿1 router, thus avoiding any cyclic dependencies on buffering
resources and requiring only a single virtual channel (VC).
2) Valiant random routing: Although intra-SN networks are
non-blocking, congestion may occur on inter-SN channels. There-
fore, the Valiant routing [44] is required to achieve load balancing
under adversarial traffic patterns. The Valiant routing for ZF is de-
fined as follows: If the destination router and the source router are
not in the same SN, a random intermediate group, which is neither
in the source SN nor the destination SN, is selected. The packet is
first routed minimally to the intermediate group and then routed
minimally again to the destination router. Notably, as illustrated
by the green path in Figure 5, the Valiant path does not need to
reach the 𝐿2 router of the intermediate group, resulting in only 6
hops, which is the same as the longest non-minimal path in DF
[49], MF [23, 42], and HX-3 [12] networks. Valiant routing requires
2 VCs, with the VC used by the packet ascending after reaching the
intermediate group.
If the destination router and the source router are within the
same SN, the Valiant algorithm continues to use minimal routing
since routing traffic to another SN offers no benefit.
3) Adaptive routing: The steps of the Sub-Network Adaptive
Load-Balancing (SNAL) are as follows.
1. If the destination router and the source router are located
within the same SN, employ minimal routing; otherwise:
2. Route to a random 𝐿1 router within the group and generate
multiple candidate paths, including both minimal and non-minimal
paths. Subsequently, evaluate the congestion along each path and
route the packet along the path with the least congestion.
Various methods can be employed when assessing path con-
gestion. By default, SNAL uses the algorithm from UGAL [43] to
evaluate path congestion, defined as:

3. If the destination router is within the current SN, SNAL em-

directing the packet along the path with the least congestion.
3.3
Advantages of Adaptive Routing in Zettafly
1) Perfect network isolation for small jobs: As shown in
Figures 5 and 6, Zettafly’s non-minimal paths do not utilize the
intra-group channels of intermediate groups. This means that for
any small jobs deployed solely within a single group, SNAL rout-
ing ensures perfect network isolation, as non-minimal traffic does
not compete for intra-group local bandwidth. However, adaptive
routing in DF, MF, and HX does not offer this feature.
2) More precise congestion awareness: UGAL [43] has been
widely adopted as the default adaptive routing algorithm for var-
ious network topologies [14, 32–36], and has been deployed in
real-world systems [13, 20, 21]. UGAL’s performance is primarily
constrained by two factors: difficulty in detecting remote conges-
tion through local queues, and an inherent bias towards paths with
shorter queue lengths. Regarding the first point, from the DF per-
spective, congestion typically occurs on the global channel of the
minimal path, which, due to topological characteristics, may not be
directly connected to the source router. This makes it challenging
for the source router to accurately detect congestion on remote
global channels through local queues [24, 28, 30, 31, 49]. For MF, the
situation is even more challenging, as the minimal global channel
is never directly connected to the source router. Moreover, adaptive
routing decisions must still be made at the source (leaf) router. Since
only a single spine router possesses the minimal global channel to
reach the destination group, the source router cannot arbitrarily
select an uplink and delegate the adaptive routing decision to the
spine router. For HX, congestion may occur across multiple remote
dimensions, which cannot be directly sensed from local queues.
Although this issue can be resolved by employing incremental
adaptive routing [39], where routing decisions are re-evaluated at
each hop, the implementation of such routing would significantly
increase the cost and latency of the routers.
For the second factor, due to physical layout, local channels have
significantly shorter physical lengths compared to global chan-
nels. Consequently, the buffers corresponding to the local channels
on the routers are smaller, and the queues are shorter. Therefore,
according to Equation 11, when the first hop of candidate paths
uses different types of channels, UGAL naturally favors the paths
where the first hop uses local channels [49]. However, the above
two issues do not arise in Zettafly. In Zettafly, the only potential
congestion points are the channels across SNs, which are always di-
rectly connected to the 𝐿1 routers. As a result, 𝐿1 routers in Zettafly
can intuitively detect congestion and make more accurate adaptive
routing decisions. Additionally, the first hop of the set of candidate
paths can only traverse a single type of channel. During intra-group
adaptive routing, the candidate paths consist entirely of local chan-
nels, while in inter-group routing, they can only be global channels.
3) Fewer memory and computation consumption: In adap-
tive routing, saving even a single VC is beneficial as it reduces the
consumption of expensive buffers. In Zettafly, SNAL employs only 2
or 3 VCs, which is fewer than DF (4 VCs) and HX-3 (6 VCs). Another
complexity of adaptive routing lies in the precise calculation of path
hop counts to evaluate congestion along the route (See Equation 11).
Inaccurate hop count calculations can negatively impact the perfor-
mance of adaptive routing [49]. However, hop count calculations
are unnecessary in Zettafly-4, as the hop counts for minimal and
non-minimal paths are fixed. In contrast, calculating hop counts
in DF and HX is not straightforward, requiring additional lookup
tables or computational operations.
Overall, the SNAL routing designed for Zettafly offers multiple
advantages. In the next section, we will conduct comprehensive
experiments to demonstrate its superior performance.

Real Workload Evaluation
We utilize the GPCNet [18] program to evaluate the network perfor-
mance of various topologies. We employ a custom-designed testing
program to generate random ring traffic and allreduce communi-
cation. Each node executes a single process. The latency statistics
in the test results are obtained by measuring the time taken for
a message to travel from the point it enters the sender’s NIC to
the point it is written into the memory of the receiver’s NIC. This
duration includes the waiting time caused by congestion control
scheduling within the NIC, the time required for memory read and
write operations, as well as the time for packet segmentation and
assembly. All networks use the DCQCN [52] congestion control
protocol, with each router port having a buffer size of 76 KB. The
RDMA NIC supports up to 256 connections, and when connection
resources are exhausted, requests are queued. The NIC and link
bandwidth are set at 100 Gbps.
Following the GPCNet standard testing setup, we randomly se-
lect 20% of nodes (referred to as the S group) to perform random
ring and allreduce communication. The remaining 80% of the nodes
(referred to as the C group) are used to generate network congestion.
During testing, nodes in the S group initially execute the expected
tests in isolation, without any network congestion. Once the iso-
lated tests are completed, the network is flushed, and the nodes in
the C group begin injecting congestion. After the network warms
up, the nodes in the S group execute the tests again.
Although GPCNet is often used to evaluate the performance
of congestion control protocols, the results are also influenced by
topology and routing algorithm. Our focus is on tail latency (99%)
in communication. We measure changes in the tail latency of the
S group before and after congestion is introduced to calculate the
GPCNet congestion factor, which serves as the final result for evalu-
ating network performance. Due to our simulator’s comprehensive
modeling of the entire GPCNet testing process, we have reduced

Discussions
In this section, we utilize a weighted cost model to demonstrate the
cost-effectiveness of Zettafly under the mixed traffic pattern. We

packaging and wiring.

5.3
Job Placement
Due to potential system fragmentation, any job smaller than a
single SN may not always be placed entirely within a single SN. To
quantify the proportion of small and medium-sized jobs that can be
isolated within a single SN under realistic scenarios, we reallocate
approximately 44K jobs from Theta’s 2023 job logs [7] onto a ZF
network based on the topology-aware job placement algorithm.
We define the job placement algorithm of ZF as follows: first, the
system attempts to place the job entirely within a single SN. If
unsuccessful, fill the SN with the most available nodes, designating
it as the job’s primary SN, then place overflow nodes in other SNs
to increase bandwidth across the primary SN. Job packing and
ordering is a complex process. We assume that Theta’s scheduler
has already compactly scheduled and ordered jobs to maximize
system utilization. Consequently, in our simulations, jobs are placed
sequentially according to their start time, as recorded in the logs,
rather than their submission time. We construct a ZF network of
equivalent size to the Theta system (N = 4,392) and assume that
the network is evenly divided into 𝑠non-blocking SNs. Our study
focuses on the following four key metrics:
T1: The number of jobs whose sizes are smaller than an SN.
A1: The number of jobs placed within an SN during a simulation.
T2: The system runtime occupied by jobs smaller than an SN.
A2: The system runtime occupied by jobs placed within an SN
during a simulation.

indicates that the algorithm has successfully placed all jobs smaller
than a single SN entirely within the SN. Clearly, this is impossible.
We additionally define two metrics to evaluate the efficiency of the
job placement algorithm: R1 = A1/T1, R2 = A2/T2.

5.4
Connections between Sub-Networks
In constructing a ZF network, there are minimal constraints on the
number of ports per router. However, we recommend using routers
with the maximum number of ports possible, as long as the single-
port bandwidth is satisfied. This approach minimizes the number of
SNs within the ZF network and maximizes the bandwidth between
these SNs. Subsequently, we can determine the number of nodes
and SNs based on the system’s predicted peak performance. In
this case, the global ports of a single 𝐿1 router may not be evenly
distributed among all SNs. For example, consider a ZF-4 network
constructed with 64-port routers and comprising four SNs, where
each 𝐿1 router’s 32 global ports need to connect to global routers
leading to the remaining three SNs. Each 𝐿1 router will have at least
10 ports directed to any other single SN. For the remaining 2 ports,
we suggest connecting them evenly to the other SNs. Connecting
global links as uniformly as possible ensures that different SN pairs
differ by at most one global link. However, there might still be
global ports that cannot pair with other SNs. Global routers can be
used to connect these ports independently.
5.5
SN-Level Incremental Deployment
In production-level systems, cost considerations often lead to the co-
existence of various generations of computational acceleration hard-
ware within many clusters [15, 40, 51]. Existing research [16, 47]
indicates that, through effective task planning and traffic sched-
uling, systems incorporating multiple generations of acceleration
hardware can still achieve high utilization rates. Consequently, in-
cremental deployment and upgrades of the systems can yield better
cost-efficiency. Similar to a fat-tree network, ZF not only effectively
supports group-level incremental deployment but also facilitates
SN-level incremental deployment.
Figure 11 illustrates the process of expanding an existing satu-
rated FT-3 system by adding an SN to build a larger system, assum-
ing we cannot purchase an entirely new FT-3 system. The original
fat-tree network can be viewed as consisting of two SNs. During
the upgrade, most global links remain unchanged, with only 25%
(4/16) of the global links needing to be interrupted. These links
will be repurposed to connect 𝑆𝑁0 and 𝑆𝑁2. Subsequently, newly
acquired global routers will be used to connect 𝑆𝑁1 and 𝑆𝑁2.
Importantly, this entire upgrade process does not require any
downtime for the existing fat-tree system and does not have any
adverse effect on 𝑆𝑁0, which remains non-blocking. 𝑆𝑁1, however,
will experience a 2:1 oversubscription. For demonstration purposes,
the routers shown in Figure 11 have only 4 ports. When considering
real-world routers with port counts such as 64, each 𝐿1 router in
a ZF-4 system with 3 SNs has 32 global ports, with each set of 16
ports connecting to the other two SNs. As we continue to add an SN,
we can disconnect a small portion of these 16 ports and use them
along with new global routers to establish connections to the fourth
SN. The entire system will experience oversubscription during
this upgrade process but will not require downtime. Additionally,

5.6
Packaging and Wiring Complexity
ZF-4 is similar to FT-3, which already has a mature packaging strat-
egy. The intra-group structures of ZF-3 and DF are identical, but
the wiring complexity is simplified in ZF-3. If all global routers are
densely packaged within several communication cabinets located
centrally in the room, then all global links will be uniformly con-
nected to these cabinets. Compared to DF, this setup would reduce
the average length of global links, thereby decreasing the latency
of global links. The introduction of communication cabinets can
also more effectively support multi-core fiber technology [36, 37],
further reducing the cost and complexity of wiring.

Related Work
Network noise: Network noise refers to the external impact on
application performance caused by other applications that share the
same network resources [19]. Network noise is widely observed in
simulation experiments and production-level systems [18, 20, 26],
and can significantly degrade the system’s performance. Adaptive
routing has been identified as a key factor contributing to network
noise [19], and reducing the non-minimal routing traffic can effec-
tively mitigate its impact. The multi-SN feature of ZF, along with
high inter-SN bandwidth and efficient adaptive routing strategies,
ensures that ZF experiences minimal network noise.
Commercial interconnection solutions: Many companies
have released comprehensive networking solutions for construct-
ing large AI systems, such as NVIDIA [4], Alibaba [41], Google
[29], and Meta [3]. Except for Google, the network topologies are
essentially fat-tree structures. This is orthogonal to our work. The
aim of Zettafly is to build a non-blocking region with full bisec-
tion bandwidth that is as large as possible, and then connect these
NBRs appropriately. For ZF-4, its NBRs are similar to fat-trees;
thus, specialized techniques used in the aforementioned intercon-
nection solutions to optimize fat-trees, such as Dual-ToR [2], Rail
Optimization [48], can be effectively adapted to ZF-4.
Advanced optical and packaging technologies: Optical Cir-
cuit Switches (OCS) typically feature hundreds of ports and do not
require additional optical transceivers. The introduction of OCS
in Zettafly, replacing the existing global routers, will significantly
reduce costs by saving half of the optical transceivers and the ma-
jority of the global routers, ultimately forming a network similar to
[22]. However, OCS has considerable link-switching overhead and
lacks efficient link allocation algorithms. Co-Packaged Optics (CPO
[45]) technology can substantially increase inter-chip transmission
bandwidth and significantly reduce power consumption. However,
it is orthogonal to the design of topology. Recently, a wafer-scale
switch [17] with thousands of ports has been proposed, which has a
power consumption of tens of kilowatts and occupies cabinet-level
space. With an extremely high number of ports, only two network
layers are required to interconnect tens of millions of nodes, fun-
damentally challenging previous topology designs. Nevertheless,
numerous technical challenges exist, and wafer-scale switches are
unlikely to be realized in the short term.

Conclusion
Based on the distribution characteristics of job sizes in real AI
and HPC systems, we propose Zettafly. It features multiple large
non-blocking sub-networks that enable the majority of jobs to be
effectively isolated within a single sub-network. Extensive experi-
ments and analysis demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art
topologies, Zettafly achieves an excellent balance between low
diameter, high bandwidth, scalability, non-blocking regions, and
cost-effectiveness. We believe it will support the development of
future large-scale interconnection systems.

Abstract: Interconnection networks are playing an increasingly crucial role in achieving scalability and throughput for post-exascale and zettas- cale computing systems. Resource consumption characteristics of AI and HPC workloads are essential to designing effective network infrastructure. The operation practice of production supercomput- ing systems reveals that small and medium-sized jobs consume most compute-core hours, generating traffic that mainly utilizes a size-restricted portion of the network. Unfortunately, current topologies lack sufficient support for flexible partitioning of dis- tinct concurrent jobs. This study bridges this gap by exploring a new tradeoff among scalability, throughput, and non-blocking re- gions. We present Zettafly, a family of low-diameter topologies with large-scale non-blocking sub-networks, allowing the majority of jobs to be isolated within a single sub-network. Zettafly is a two-layer structure, consisting of non-blocking groups and global routers, such that each minimally routed packet between groups traverses at most one global router. We also introduce simple and efficient adaptive routing algorithms for Zettafly. We conduct exten- sive simulations and analysis to evaluate the performance and cost of Zettafly against state-of-the-art topologies. The results show that Zettafly achieves great performance under typical HPC workloads, offers cost-effectiveness under multi-task mixed traffic, supports flexible configurations and incremental deployments, and is cost- effective to deploy for post-exascale and zettascale systems.
